body:
in Comics/Cartoons, Music |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a pro­duc­er, arranger, and jazz com­pos­er. And while he’s best known for arrang­ing music for Bil­lie Hol­i­day’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orches­trat­ing music for tele­vi­sion. Work­ing under a pseu­do­nym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis com­posed back­ground music for the car­toon stu­dio Fil­ma­tion between 1968 and 1982. And, dur­ing the late 60s, he notably cre­at­ed the back­ground and inci­den­tal music for the orig­i­nal Spi­der-Man car­toons.
Above, hear Ray Ellis’ Spi­der-Man sound­track. The show’s talk­ing parts and sound effects have been removed as much as pos­si­ble, then “pieced back togeth­er into com­plete form,” by a YouTu­ber who uses the moniker “11db11.” All of the music from Sea­son 1 is includ­ed, plus many record­ings from Sea­sons 2 and 3. It’s worth not­ing that the 52 episodes from the orig­i­nal 1967 Spi­der-Man TV series have been com­plete­ly restored. You can pur­chase them on DVD online.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: Harry Houdini Died 100 Years Ago This Halloween: Was He Really Killed by a Punch to the Stomach?
description:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­r
body:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­ry Hou­di­ni. Today, most of us know more about the man­ner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the sto­ry goes, he’d mas­tered his own body to the extent that he could tight­en his abdom­i­nal mus­cles so as to with­stand even the hard­est punch to the gut. Or at least that’s the image he let cir­cu­late: tak­ing it as a chal­lenge, a stu­dent and ama­teur box­er turned up and offered his fist to Hou­di­ni as an unex­pect­ed test. A week and a half lat­er, the great escapol­o­gist was dead of peri­toni­tis.
It seemed that the blow he sus­tained had rup­tured Hou­dini’s already-inflamed appen­dix, and that remained the wide­ly accept­ed, if not med­ical­ly air­tight, expla­na­tion for near­ly a cen­tu­ry. Yet there was always some­thing too dra­mat­i­cal­ly neat in the tale of a man famed for defy­ing death being done in by noth­ing more than a thought­less young man’s suck­er punch. Gen­er­a­tions of enthu­si­asts have offered expla­na­tions of their own, some more plau­si­ble than oth­ers, but few inves­ti­ga­tions into this qua­si-leg­endary demise have been con­duct­ed as seri­ous­ly as the one under­tak­en in our time by retired urol­o­gist Lar­ri­an Gille­spie, author of Hou­di­ni: The Man Who Died Twice.
When she had the chance to exam­ine his death cer­tifi­cate, Gille­spie noticed appar­ent irreg­u­lar­i­ties that led her down the rab­bit hole to “a paper trail of mis­state­ments and actions by more than a dozen peo­ple close to Hou­di­ni, includ­ing rel­a­tives and employ­ees,” writes the New York Times’ Robin Pogre­bin, “includ­ing a con­spir­a­cy to change his offi­cial death date to Octo­ber 31st, fix­ing his mem­o­ry to Hal­loween.” Accord­ing to her recon­struc­tion of events, Hou­di­ni actu­al­ly died the day before: not of appen­dici­tis, and not as a result of the young man’s punch. “Rather, she argues, the cul­prit was a bow­el obstruc­tion, brought on by a fibrous mass of chop suey that Hou­di­ni ate on Oct. 28.”


	

Emer­gency surgery took place the next day, but it was too late. “Sep­tic shock set in, Houdini’s fever spiked to 105 and his rapid breath­ing led to mus­cle spasms and uncon­scious­ness.” He was oper­at­ed on again the day after, and “Gillespie’s research into the death cer­tifi­cates indi­cates that the magi­cian died that after­noon at 1:26 p.m.” Gille­spie argues that the lack of a prop­er autop­sy helped con­ceal pos­si­ble med­ical mal­prac­tice and allowed Hou­dini’s wid­ow to col­lect a dou­ble-indem­ni­ty pay­ment for what was treat­ed as an acci­den­tal death. Even if accept­ed, her the­o­ry prob­a­bly won’t erase the cul­tur­al link between Hou­di­ni and Hal­loween. But the the­o­ry does add a new dimen­sion of irony to his life sto­ry: the man who could sur­vive a Chi­nese water tor­ture cell proved to be no match for Amer­i­can Chi­nese food.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Wish You Were Here! Rose Sanderson's Witty Postcards Conjure a Strange Reality
description: Like many artists, Rose Sanderson began a body of work during the early days of the pandemic as a sort of balm for the harsh realities of the worl
body:
Like many artists, Rose Sanderson began a body of work during the early days of the pandemic as a sort of balm for the harsh realities of the world. “I started playing with escapism and imagination, mixing reality and fiction, and the blurring of childhood memories and nostalgia,” she says of her surreal paintings on vintage postcards. “Many of the images are in seaside towns, influenced by growing up in one myself through the ’80s and ’90s.”
Playing with scale, Sanderson renders scenes that evoke the Creature Features of early cinema: an enormous crab is on the verge of scuttling over a beach filled with people, a tiger lounges alongside an unsuspecting man, and a zig-zagged fissure bisects the ground around an amusement park. But thanks to the artist’s wit, the paintings are more humorous than horrifying, plunging viewers into a bizarre dreamland where the uncanny is always lurking around the corner.
“Shipping hazard”
Sanderson has been collecting the postcards from thrift stores, antique shops, markets, and online retailers for several years, which she’s added to a collection started by her grandparents. “There is something special about these snippets of history that give me a warm fuzzy feeling, and I love a lot of the aged, saturated colours, too.” 
Having reached 50 paintings, Sanderson’s series will be on view from November 11 to December 23 at Aberystwyth Arts Centre. A limited-edition book featuring all of the works will be available as well. Follow along for updates on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Scott Kahn Invokes Dreams and Liminality in Atmospheric Landscape Paintings
description: Until a few years ago, painter Scott Kahn was living in his cousin’s attic, with a studio filled with work that he hadn’t had a lot of luck sellin
body:
Until a few years ago, painter Scott Kahn was living in his cousin’s attic, with a studio filled with work that he hadn’t had a lot of luck selling. Then, he began a chance correspondence with the late Canadian artist Matthew Wong, who related to Kahn’s own self-taught background and interest in magical realism. “Matthew was really a great champion of my work,” Kahn told Artnet News. “The only way I can explain it is that we were soulmates.” When Wong’s career took off in 2018, Kahn’s atmospheric, often surreal landscapes also found their audience.
Mostly working in oil on linen, Kahn creates scenes that glow beneath the bright moon or complement architectural elements seen through vignettes of trees and clouds. The works shown here were recently on view in the artist’s sweeping solo exhibition, Silent Night at David Zwirner.
“Berkshire Nightscape II” (2005), oil on linen, 36 1/8 x 40 inches
We encounter nods to American regionalism, such as in “Berkshire Nightscape II” with its pronounced resemblance to Grant Wood’s bulbous, cultivated hills of rural Iowa. Other works invoke the realm of the unconscious, such “The Basement Window,” which recalls a recurring dream the artist has of his childhood home. Trees appear both inside and outside, blurring the boundary between architectural space and nature. In “The Stoop,” a mysterious, deep-forest darkness infringes upon the sunniness of front steps.
In “The Basement,” there is also a subtle connection to the interiority of the body in the trees’ vein-like branches and roots. Through structural apertures, such as a window or a balcony—including the paintings’ inherent frames—the surrounding environment is open to us but always limited. There is always a compelling edge, horizon, shadow, or disappearing path that prompts us to question whether we can truly comprehend what we see.
Kahn’s compositions often feel familiar, yet through deep contrasts, long shadows, nighttime scenes, and portal-like framing, he invokes a sense of enigma and liminality. The scenes are often stretched, as if seen through a wide-angle lens, and there is an indelible sense of transition, whether from night to day, sleeping to waking, or imagination to reality. “I don’t get too bogged down in what a landscape actually is,” Kahn says. “It’s more a vehicle to express a mood. That, to me, is the value of a landscape.”
See more on the artist’s Instagram.
“Leap from the Balcony” (2003), oil on linen, 61 7/8 x 72 inches
“The Stoop” (2024/2025), oil on wood panel, 28 x 22 inches
“The Basement” (2025), oil on linen, 52 1/4 x 60 1/4 inches
“New Moon” (2008/2013), oil on linen, 18 x 20 inches

title: Artists Take to the Streets Amid Massive Protests in France
description:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector c
body:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector coalitions demanding a better life for artists. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Artists, art students, and cultural workers joined hundreds of thousands of protesters marching across France on October 24, 2026. (photo Nicolas Tucat / AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            PARIS — On the heels of last Saturday’s mass protests — and amid the preemptive closure of Art Basel Paris and museums like the Louvre — Paris’s artists, culture workers, and art students were back in the streets today, October 24. Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie for a march called in part by Cultures en Lutte, the network of culture-sector coalitions that has mobilized alongside the labor confederations and student unions since the movement began in mid-September, and by one of its driving forces, the National Union of Visual Artists (SNAP-CGT).  They came despite a week of warnings. After the destruction of October 17, the French government announced a “massive” security deployment: Sentinelle anti-terror soldiers would relieve police of guard duties, while special units would be backed by helicopters, armored vehicles, and water cannons. More than 250,000 protestors turned out anyway in Paris, and several hundred thousand more around the country, reports estimate. Police arrested approximately 1,000 protesters just today.  A painted sign depicts French President Emmanuel Macron using "our rights" as toilet paper.Students pose with their signs at the October 24 protest. The left sign warns against the use of AI; the right sign reads, “The boat is sinking, but the politicians are fighting over who will be captain.”

title: The Artist Who Dined Among Lions
description:
Art Review
                California performance artist Bonnie Ora Sherk was a cultural trickster and proactive spoiler in the
body:
Art Review
                California performance artist Bonnie Ora Sherk was a cultural trickster and proactive spoiler in the business of everyday life. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Bonnie Ora Sherk, "Sitting Still" (1970), projection of Kodachrome photograph (all photos courtesy Brian Karl/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            SANTA BARBARA — People didn’t always live in cities. It became more of the norm as asphalt and concrete covered dirt, and highways and overpasses became the infrastructure for commuting and delivering food and supplies. Bonnie Ora Sherk (1945–2021) spent four decades as an artist, landscape designer, and educator challenging the assumptions that underpin city life. Through her creative projects, Sherk consistently proposed new models of social relations. The retrospective Life Frames since 1970 at the University of California, Santa Barbara’s Museum of Art, Design, and Architecture, is a well-designed, if modest, exhibition that highlights many of her interventions, from performances to interactive engagements, as documented in drawings, posters, photographs, and moving images. Sherk began as a cultural trickster, like many conceptually based artists from the late 1950s onward, often acting as both observer and observed — and proactive spoiler — in the business of everyday life. After studying with Fluxus artists Robert Watts and Mel Henderson, Sherk applied a post-Dadaist performance sensibility to visionary yet practical rethinking of human priorities, promoting mindful encounters with other living creatures. Because much of the exhibition is documentary, the aesthetics are somewhat limited, with occasional visual pleasures. Set in mundane outdoor locations in San Francisco, Sherk’s series Sitting Still (1970) — in which the artist places herself in ordinary chairs amid daily urban life — is presented in the exhibition through projections of large-scale Kodachrome photographs. Nearby, a black-and-white film transferred to video documents “Public Lunch” (1971), projecting Sherk caged in the San Francisco Zoo’s Lion House next to big cats in a neighboring lockup, as visitors gawked while both cats and the artist paced, napped, and were fed. Bonnie Ora Sherk, "Public Lunch" (1971), video installation

title: From Paris, In Solidarity
description:
Daily Newsletter
                Surreal scenes from an art week amid protests, lessons from the NEA Four, and Kid Cudi’s Basqui
body:
Daily Newsletter
                Surreal scenes from an art week amid protests, lessons from the NEA Four, and Kid Cudi’s Basquiat biopic.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            When journalist Naima Morelli arrived in Paris last weekend, she could smell the scent of burning plastic in the air. Thus began her quest to report on the city’s surreal week of exhibitions and blue-chip art fairs, with million-dollar artworks changing hands as students protest deteriorating education and public service systems. Morelli captures the atmosphere, both dystopian and hopeful, in her dispatch below.In another city with a rich history of protest, New York performance artist Martha Wilson reviews a history of the Culture Wars told in Isaac Butler’s new book The Perfect Moment, reflecting on the work of the NEA Four, David Wojnarowicz, and other artists who defended creative expression in a time not unlike our own. Also today, Duaa Shah takes a deep-dive into the way art circulates in the legal system as both treatment and evidence, particularly for displaced communities seeking justice.More, as always, including a review of the Toronto Biennial and the unlikely star of a new Jean-Michel Basquiat biopic: Kid Cudi.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

	
		
			Portrait of a Paris Art Week on Fire
		
	
	
		“The people in the art world are courageous,” a collector told me at Asia Now, the first of the Paris art fairs that opened early in the week on Monday, in the heat of the protests. “But I would still like to be back at my hotel before 7pm, you know, just in case.”

Anyone who is a regular at Paris Art Week has a collection of stories about something going wrong. In 2022, there were strikes and cost-of-living marches. In October 2023, France was on high terror alert, and one of the bomb threats that emptied the airports of the country’s major cities led to, among other things, my plane landing in the middle of the French countryside. A couple of trains later, and voilà: I was in Paris in time for the vernissages. | Naima Morelli
	
	
		Read More
	



                    
                    
                    
                        
                            Tuan Andrew Nguyen: Transforming Remnants of War into Objects for Healing Tuan Andrew Nguyen’s fourth solo exhibition with Norr Cohan, Sacred Forest / Rừng Thiêng, opens October 30 and will be on view through December 19, 2026, at the gallery’s 48 & 52 Walker Street locations. The exhibition will premiere a new film alongside suspended mobiles and a monumental stabile that extends the artist’s engagement with the people of the Quảng Trị region in Vietnam, whose lives are forever altered by the presence of unexploded ordnance.

                            Skirball Cultural Center presents “The 1960s — A Generation on Fire: Judy Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles”The exhibition shares two new sections of the public art mural on view for the first time, featuring moments from an era of collective action that still resonates today.

			The War on Art Is Repeating Itself
		
	
	
		As an artist who lived through the Reagan-era Culture Wars, I recommend Isaac Butler’s “The Perfect Moment” for the stories that parallel our current fight to defend creative expression. | Martha Wilson
